description: Animal communication's four limited functions, Von Frisch's bee study, and human language.
content_html:
Animal Communication Versus Human Communication

All animals communicate in some way — from the alarm calls of meerkats to the song of birds. But how different is animal communication from the language used by humans? Psychologists and biologists have studied this question carefully, and the evidence points to some fundamental differences in both the functions and properties of communication across species.

The Limited Functions of Animal Communication

Animal communication serves a small set of essential functions. The spec identifies four: survival, reproduction, territory and food. These functions are directly linked to biological drives and immediate circumstances.

Animals signal danger to alert group members to predators (survival); display to attract mates or warn off rivals (reproduction); mark boundaries and warn intruders away (territory); and direct group members to food sources (food). These signals are highly effective within their narrow purpose, but they are tied to the present situation rather than to abstract thinking.

Key Fact

Animal communication is limited to four functions: survival (alerting to danger), reproduction (attracting mates), territory (marking boundaries) and food (signalling food location). These are tied to immediate biological needs rather than abstract or flexible communication.

Von Frisch’s Bee Study

Karl von Frisch conducted pioneering research into animal communication, studying how honeybees communicate the location of food sources to other members of the hive. This is one of the most remarkable examples of animal communication documented by researchers.

Aim: Von Frisch aimed to investigate how honeybees communicate the location and distance of food sources to other bees in the hive.

Method: Von Frisch observed bees returning to the hive after finding food. He watched their movement patterns inside the hive and related these ‘dances’ to the location and distance of the food source he had set up at known positions.

Results: Von Frisch found that returning bees performed two distinct dances. A round dance indicated that food was within approximately 50–100 metres of the hive. A waggle dance (a figure-of-eight pattern with a straight waggle run in the middle) indicated food at a greater distance (beyond approximately 100 metres). The angle of the waggle run corresponded to the direction of the food relative to the sun, and the duration of the waggle run corresponded to the distance to the food — a longer waggle run indicating greater distance.

Conclusion: Von Frisch concluded that bees can communicate specific information about the direction and distance of a food source using a coded system of movement. This is a sophisticated form of animal communication — but it is still limited to the function of communicating about food and is not flexible or generative like human language.

Key Fact

Von Frisch found bees use a round dance for nearby food and a waggle dance for distant food. The waggle dance encodes direction (angle relative to the sun) and distance (duration of the waggle run). This is sophisticated but limited to communicating about food.

Properties of Human Communication Not Present in Animals

Human language has properties that set it apart from even the most complex animal communication systems. The spec highlights the ability to plan ahead and discuss future events as a key distinguishing feature.

Animal communication is largely tied to the here and now. A bee cannot tell the hive “there will be nectar in three days when the flowers bloom.” A vervet monkey cannot warn others that a predator was there yesterday. Human language, by contrast, can discuss things that are distant in time (past and future), abstract concepts, hypothetical situations (“what if”), fiction, and ideas with no physical referent at all.

Human language is also productive: using a finite set of words and grammar rules, humans can create and understand an unlimited number of new sentences they have never encountered before. Animal communication systems typically have a fixed number of signals that cannot be recombined to create new meanings.

Human language is learnt rather than entirely innate: while humans have a biological capacity for language, the specific language spoken is acquired from the social environment. Different human communities use entirely different languages — a contrast to animal communication systems, which are largely species-specific and appear to be mainly instinctive.

A strength of Von Frisch’s research is that it used careful observation over many years, with controlled manipulation of food source positions, allowing the relationship between dance patterns and location to be mapped systematically. The findings have been replicated and have had significant impact on our understanding of animal behaviour.

A limitation is that even Von Frisch’s sophisticated example of bee communication is still limited to one function (food), one context (the hive), and one species. Trying to compare animal communication directly with human language is difficult because they are fundamentally different systems serving different purposes — it may not be a fair comparison to judge animal communication as ‘inferior’ when it perfectly serves its adaptive purpose.
exam_tip_html: For ‘describe a study’ questions on Von Frisch, remember to include both dances and what each indicates. A common mistake is just mentioning the waggle dance and forgetting the round dance, or confusing which indicates nearness and which indicates distance. Aim: near food = round; far food = waggle (with angle = direction, duration = distance).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Animal communication is limited to four functions: survival, reproduction, territory and food — all tied to immediate biological needs and the present context.
  • Von Frisch found honeybees use a round dance for nearby food and a waggle dance (encoding direction and distance) for food further away — sophisticated, but limited to one function.
  • Human language differs from animal communication in its ability to discuss future events, past events, abstract concepts and hypothetical situations — and in its productiveness and cultural learning.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is NOT a function of animal communication identified in the specification?
A) Survival
B) Reproduction
C) Planning future events
D) Territory
practice_questions.marks: C) Planning future events [1 mark] — this is a property of human communication not present in animal communication.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'waggle dance' as used in Von Frisch's bee study.
practice_questions.marks: The waggle dance is a figure-of-eight movement performed by a honeybee [1 mark] in which the angle of the straight waggle run indicates the direction of a food source relative to the sun, and the duration indicates its distance from the hive [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Describe three ways in which human communication differs from animal communication.
practice_questions.marks: Any three from: humans can plan ahead and discuss future events (animals cannot — they are tied to the present) [1 mark]; human language is productive — an unlimited number of novel sentences can be created (animals have a fixed signal repertoire) [1 mark]; human language is culturally learned (the specific language depends on the environment) whereas animal communication is largely innate and species-specific [1 mark]. Accept other relevant distinctions with development.

practice_questions.text: A researcher studies how wolves howl to communicate with each other. Using your knowledge of animal communication, explain what functions this communication is likely to serve and what it cannot do.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies two of the four limited functions (e.g. territory — howls mark pack boundaries and warn off rival packs; survival — howls can alert pack members to danger) explicitly linked to the wolf example; explains what the communication cannot do (e.g. wolves cannot discuss future events or hypothetical situations, showing the limitation of animal communication compared to human language).
Secure: One function identified and explained, and one limitation noted.
Developing: Names a function without fully explaining it, or mentions limitation vaguely.
Emerging: Vague reference to animal communication without specific functions or limitations.

practice_questions.text: Describe Von Frisch's bee study of animal communication.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate aim (how bees communicate food location/distance), method (observation of returning forager bees in the hive), results (round dance = nearby food; waggle dance = distant food with angle = direction relative to sun, duration = distance), and conclusion (bees use a coded movement system to communicate food location, though limited to food function) — all four elements.
Secure: Three elements described accurately.
Developing: Two elements or one in good detail; some inaccuracy.
Emerging: Vague account with limited specific detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the differences between human and animal communication.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate description of animal communication (four limited functions, fixed signals, tied to present context); Von Frisch's bee study as evidence; properties of human communication not in animals (planning ahead, discussing future/past, abstract topics, productivity, cultural learning); evaluation includes at least two developed points (e.g. Von Frisch shows animal communication can be sophisticated and symbolic, yet still limited; comparing them may be unfair as both serve their purpose; human language's productivity is qualitatively different).
Secure: Description of most content; evaluation covers two points with some development.
Developing: Describes some differences; evaluation underdeveloped.
Emerging: Brief description; minimal evaluation.

knowledge_checks.q: What does the round dance in Von Frisch's study signal to other bees?
options: Food is far away from the hive
Food is close to the hive

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is a property of human communication NOT found in animal communication?
In the waggle dance, the _____ of the waggle run indicates how far away the food source is.
Animal communication is limited to four functions: survival, reproduction, _____ and food.
Match each dance to what it communicates in Von Frisch's study:
right: Food source is located close to the hive
Food source is at a greater distance, with direction and distance encoded

flashcard_questions.q: What are the four limited functions of animal communication?
What was the aim of Von Frisch's bee study?
flashcard_questions.a: To investigate how honeybees communicate the location and distance of food sources.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the round dance indicate in Von Frisch's study?
flashcard_questions.a: Food is located close to the hive.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the waggle dance indicate in Von Frisch's study?
flashcard_questions.a: Food is at a greater distance from the hive.

flashcard_questions.q: In the waggle dance, what does the angle of the waggle run indicate?
flashcard_questions.a: The direction of the food source relative to the sun.

flashcard_questions.q: In the waggle dance, what does the duration of the waggle run indicate?
flashcard_questions.a: The distance to the food source.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Von Frisch conclude from his bee study?
flashcard_questions.a: Bees use a coded dance system to communicate direction and distance of food, but only for food.

flashcard_questions.q: What key ability of human communication is absent in animal communication?
flashcard_questions.a: Planning ahead and discussing future or past events and abstract ideas.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is Von Frisch's bee study considered a strength of animal communication research?
flashcard_questions.a: He used systematic observation with controlled food-source positions, allowing the link between dance patterns and location to be mapped reliably.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is productivity a uniquely human language property?
flashcard_questions.a: Humans can create unlimited new sentences; animals have a fixed repertoire of signals.

glossary_terms.definition: The four main purposes that animal communication systems typically serve.
A circular movement performed by a bee to indicate a food source close to the hive.
A figure-of-eight movement performed by a bee in which the waggle run indicates the direction and distance of a food source.

glossary_terms.term: plan ahead and discuss future events
glossary_terms.definition: The capacity of human language to communicate about events or situations that are not present in the immediate environment, including the past and future.
